scenes.name: Soul sureño: Stax, Atlantic y FAME
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Stax era un negocio familiar en un viejo cine de Memphis, de dueños blancos (Jim Stewart y Estelle Axton) con una banda de estudio integrada (Steve Cropper, Isaac Hayes, Al Jackson, Duck Dunn, Booker T.) y solo artistas negros: ritmo pesado y vientos ásperos. Jerry Wexler llevó allí a Wilson Pickett, bailó el Jerk para enseñar el contratiempo de «In the Midnight Hour» y, cuando Stax lo vetó, lo llevó a los FAME de Rick Hall en Muscle Shoals, donde acababan de grabar «When a Man Loves a Woman» de Percy Sledge. Con una banda casi toda blanca (Spooner Oldham, Roger Hawkins) y pastillas, Pickett convirtió un estándar de cuatro años en la versión definitiva de «Land of 1000 Dances» (julio de 1966): gritos afinados, ritmo frenético, el «na, na-ne-na-na», un fragmento de un show que podría durar horas; parte de un continuo de la cultura negra entre el orgullo y la rabia. Otis Redding, heredero de Sam Cooke tras su asesinato, rompió con «I’ve Been Loving You Too Long» y Otis Blue fijó la palabra «soul», pero Stax no vendía como Motown hasta que Sam & Dave triunfaron con «Hold On! I’m Comin’». Los Beatles quisieron grabar en Stax en abril de 1966; su sonido está por todo Rubber Soul. La revista de Stax en Watts coincidió con los disturbios de agosto de 1965.

scenes.name: Stax
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Otis Redding, Booker T & the MGs, Johnnie Taylor, Rufus y Carla Thomas, los Staple Singers, Isaac Hayes y Albert King, capaz de rivalizar con Motown en ventas, con un sonido campestre y frito más pensado para el público negro. Frente al montaje mecánico de Motown, en Stax se grababa todo junto: «toca lo que sientas» (Otis Redding). «Tramp» de Otis y Carla, con el bajo más grave de la radio, es proto-funk puro; Johnnie Taylor llevó la sordidez sexual al soul («Who’s Making Love», «Disco Lady» con Bootsy al bajo); Rufus Thomas, payaso de «Do the Funky Chicken», hizo un poco más aceptable ser funky. Los MGs eran groove fluido más que bomba funk («Hip Hug-Her», «Melting Pot»), y los Bar-Kays originales («Soul Finger») habrían sido reyes de Memphis si no hubieran muerto con Otis en 1967.

podcast.title: "What'd I Say" Damascene Conversion
podcast.body: Jim Stewart experienced a profound shift in his musical direction after hearing Ray Charles's "What'd I Say," produced by Jerry Wexler. This record solidified his commitment to an R&B style for his company. "He'd recently had a sort of damacine conversion after hearing that record, and was now fully committed to his company's new R&B style."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Barber's Business Advice
podcast.body: A tip from his barber, Irwin Ellis, about the lucrative nature of owning song publishing rights, rather than just selling records, significantly influenced Stewart's approach to the music business. This financial insight appealed to him given his background in banking. "Alice explained to Stuart that he was still getting checks every few months, because he owned the publishing for this song that someone else had written and wrote to him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Conflict with Chips Moman
podcast.body: Jim Stewart was involved in a dispute with Chips Moman, who claimed he had been promised a third of the company but Stewart refused. This disagreement led to Moman's departure from Stax Records. "he also claims that he had been promised a third of the company, but Jim Stewart changed his mind and refused to cut him in."

podcast.title: Early Life and Influences
podcast.body: Jim Stewart was a part-time fiddle player deeply influenced by Bob Wills' western swing music. Despite his musical passion, he worked a day job at a bank as music wasn't providing a stable income. "Stewart was in a western swing band and was hugely influenced by Bbock Will's, but he wasn't making any real money from music."

podcast.title: Founding Satellite Records
podcast.body: Stewart pooled savings with a singing DJ and a rhythm guitarist, raising $1,000 to release a record. They named their label Satellite Records, a name nobody liked but was chosen due to Sputnik's recent launch. "They came up with the name satellite records for their label. Nobody liked it, but they couldn't think of anything better, and satellites were in the news with the recent launch of Sputnik."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Reluctant Release of Otis Redding's Debut
podcast.body: Jim Stewart was initially unimpressed by Otis Redding's first recording session, describing the A-side as "a fun but unoriginal little Richard sound alike." He only agreed to release the record as a favor to promoter Joe Galkin, not anticipating the B-side would become a hit. "Jim Stewart wasn't particularly impressed with the results, but he owed Galkin a favour, so he released the record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Restarting Satellite Records
podcast.body: After initial failures and setbacks, Stewart convinced his sister Estelle Axton to buy out his business partners. With Axton's financial backing from remortgaging her house, and Chips Moman's studio expertise, Satellite Records was re-launched in a barber's storage space. "Stuart Mice persuaded his sister, Estelle Axton, to buy out his business partners."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Stax Records Name Origin
podcast.body: When Satellite Records faced a trademark conflict with another label of the same name, Jim Stewart, who disliked the original name anyway, decided to rename the label. The new name, Stax Records, was created using the first two letters of his surname (Stewart) and his sister Estelle Axton's surname. "Jim Stewart had never liked satellite as a name anyway, and so they quickly reissued the record with a new label, named after the first letters of Jim Stewart and Asterl Axton's surnames. Stax Records was born."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Wife's Uncle's Garage Studio
podcast.body: The initial recordings for Satellite Records, including Fred Byler's "Blue Roses," took place in Jim's wife's uncle's garage using Irwin Ellis's tape recorder. This makeshift studio ceased to be available when Ellis moved and the uncle needed his garage back. "they hired Alice in his tape recorder to record it in Jim's wife's uncle's garage."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Witnessing Elvis's Rise
podcast.body: Stewart had been part of a house band at a venue where Elvis Presley played in his early career. He observed Elvis's rapid ascent from an obscure local artist to a global superstar, which fueled his attraction to the music industry. "One of the gigs he'd had was in the house band at a venue where Elvis sometimes played in his early years, and he'd seen how Elvis had gone from an obscure local boy all the way to the biggest star in the world."
